While this study meets most inclusion criteria (original epidemiological study, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series design), it does not report a relative risk, odds ratio, or equivalent effect measure with confidence interval. The study only reports correlation coefficients (R values) and regression coefficients from a linear model, not the standardized effect estimates (RR/OR) required for systematic review inclusion.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as an exposure, (3) respiratory hospitalizations are reported as an outcome, (4) it uses a time-series design, (5) it reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs (1.14% increase per 10 μg/m3 PM2.5 for respiratory hospitalizations, 95% CI: 0.53%, 1.75%), and (6) the abstract is in English. The study analyzes multiple outcomes including respiratory hospitalizations specifically.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5 (fine particulate matter <2.5 microns), (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalizations (pneumonia and asthma), (4) study design is time-series, (5) reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals for multiple lag periods, and (6) appears to be published in English (or translated). The study uses appropriate statistical methods (generalized additive model with Poisson regression) and provides quantitative effect estimates.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 exposure is examined, (3) outcome is respiratory emergency department visits for pneumonia, (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., 18.2% increase, 95% CI 8.8-28.4% for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Pneumonia is a respiratory condition and ED visits are equivalent to emergency department visits.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study comparing two analytical approaches, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as an exposure, (3) respiratory disease hospitalizations are the outcome, (4) both time-series and case-crossover designs are used, (5) quantitative effect estimates are reported as percentage increases with confidence intervals for each 10 μg/m3 increment in PM2.5, and (6) the publication is in English. The study provides specific effect estimates for PM2.5 (e.g., 6.4% and 4.5% increases in Warsaw).

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as an exposure, (3) the outcome is asthma hospital admissions (a respiratory hospitalization), (4) both time-series and case-crossover designs were used, (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs are reported (e.g., 30.2% increase, 95% CI: 13.4-49.6% for PM2.5), and (6) the article is in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization (pneumonia), (4) uses appropriate time-series methodology with Poisson regression, and (5) reports quantitative effect estimates showing association between PM2.5 and hospitalizations with lag effects. While the abstract does not explicitly state RR/OR with confidence intervals, it clearly indicates statistical associations were found and quantitative estimates were calculated (256 fewer admissions per 10 µg/m3 decrease), which implies effect estimates were derived.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Original epidemiological study using GAM with Poisson distribution and DLNM; (2) Exposure is PM2.5 with five different metrics; (3) Outcome is COPD hospitalization/admission, which is a respiratory hospitalization; (4) Study design is time-series based on daily records 2018-2019; (5) Reports quantitative effect estimates as percent increases with 95% confidence intervals for all five exposure metrics; (6) Published in English. COPD hospitalization is a specific type of respiratory hospitalization that fits the outcome criteria.

This is an original time-series study that examines PM2.5 exposure (among other PM fractions) and respiratory hospital admissions. The study uses Poisson regression models and reports statistically significant associations, which implies quantitative effect estimates are provided. While the main finding for respiratory admissions was associated with PM10 and PM10-2.5 during dust intrusions, the study also analyzed PM2.5 and respiratory outcomes during non-dust periods, meeting the inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly measured as exposure, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization (asthma readmissions), (4) case-crossover design is specified, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (OR = 1.082, 95% CI = 1.008-1.162 for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Although the outcome is hospital readmissions rather than initial admissions, readmissions are still respiratory hospitalizations and meet the outcome criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original case-crossover epidemiological study, (2) examines PM2.5 exposure (along with PM10), (3) outcome is asthma-related hospital visits which are respiratory hospitalizations, (4) case-crossover design, (5) reports effect estimates with 95% CI (e.g., 1.26, 95% CI 1.22-1.30), and (6) published in English. The study analyzes both PM10 and PM2.5, with PM2.5 being one of the exposures of interest.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as an exposure alongside ozone, (3) outcome is respiratory (asthma) emergency department visits, (4) uses both time-series and case-crossover designs, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates (RR and OR) with 95% CIs for both pollutants, and (6) published in English. Although PM2.5 was not significantly associated with the outcome, the study still examined PM2.5 and reported effect estimates, making it eligible for inclusion in the systematic review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 and respiratory outcomes, (2) exposure is source-specific PM2.5, (3) outcomes include asthma and COPD hospitalizations and ED visits, (4) uses a modified time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports excess rates (ERs) with specific quantitative estimates (e.g., 0.5%-3.1%, 1.3%-1.7%, 2.1%-3.4%), and (6) published in English. The study analyzes PM2.5 from multiple sources, which is acceptable per inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of multiple exposures, (3) outcome is hospital admissions for asthma (a respiratory hospitalization), (4) case-crossover study design, (5) reports OR with 95% CI for PM2.5 (OR 1.09; 95% CI 1.04 to 1.13), and (6) published in English. Although multiple pollutants are examined, PM2.5 is specifically included and analyzed.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalizations, (4) reports quantitative effect estimates as percent increases which can be converted to relative risks, (5) appears to be published in English. The study explicitly examines PM2.5 from biomass burning and its association with hospital admissions for respiratory diseases using appropriate statistical methods.

Although this study examines PM2.5 (fine particulate matter) exposure and uses a time-series design with effect estimates, the outcome is acute otitis media (AOM) hospitalizations, not respiratory hospitalizations or ED visits. AOM is an ear infection, not a respiratory condition, despite its association with upper respiratory tract infections. This does not meet the inclusion criteria for respiratory hospitalization outcomes.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using distributed lag nonlinear models; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as an exposure; (3) the outcome is respiratory hospitalizations (pneumonia, COPD, asthma); (4) the study design is time-series based on daily admissions and air pollutant data; (5) quantitative effect estimates are reported (RR with 95% CI for PM2.5 at lag 12: RR=1.068, 95% CI 1.017-1.121); and (6) the abstract is in English. The study also examines PM10, but PM2.5 is one of the multiple exposures analyzed, which is acceptable per inclusion criteria.

This is an original case-crossover study examining the association between air pollution (including PM2.5 as one of three pollutants in the AQHI) and respiratory ED visits for asthma. The study reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Although the exposure is a composite index (AQHI) rather than PM2.5 alone, PM2.5 (fine particulate matter) is explicitly stated as one of the three pollutants included in the index, meeting the criterion that PM2.5 can be one of multiple exposures analyzed. The outcome is respiratory ED visits, the design is case-crossover, and quantitative effect estimates are provided.

While this study examines respiratory ED visits and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals, the primary exposure is thunderstorms and power outages, not PM2.5. PM2.5 is only examined as a mediating/modifying factor of the thunderstorm-health relationship, not as the main exposure of interest. The study does not provide direct PM2.5 exposure-respiratory hospitalization associations that would be relevant for a systematic review on PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as an exposure, (3) respiratory hospitalizations are the primary outcome, (4) it uses a time-series design, (5) quantitative effect estimates are reported (0.9-4.5% increase per 10 units PM2.5 increase), and (6) it is published in English. The abstract clearly states effect estimates with confidence in the statistical significance.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and adult pneumonia hospital visits including ED visits. The abstract indicates effect estimates were calculated (mentions statistically significant impacts and effect estimates), though specific numerical values are not provided in the abstract. Pneumonia hospitalizations are respiratory hospitalizations. Meets all inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (ICD-9: 460-519), (4) time-series study design explicitly stated, (5) reports RR with 95% CI for respiratory causes (RR=1.049, 95% CI 1.019-1.078), and (6) published in English. Although the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it includes respiratory hospitalizations as a separate outcome of interest.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series design with Poisson regression; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) respiratory hospitalizations among elderly are examined as an outcome; (4) the study design is time-series; (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs are reported (e.g., 23.5% increase for PM2.5-10 and respiratory diseases); (6) the article appears to be published in English. Although PM2.5 showed significant association primarily with circulatory diseases in this study, the abstract indicates that PM2.5-10 and PM10 were associated with respiratory diseases, and PM2.5 chemical constituents (K⁺) were associated with both outcomes including respiratory admissions.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using ecological time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalization among other outcomes, (4) study design is explicitly time-series, (5) the abstract indicates associations were estimated (effect estimates), and (6) appears to be published in English. While the study examines multiple outcomes (mortality and hospitalizations for various causes), respiratory hospitalization is specifically mentioned as one of the outcomes analyzed.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original time-series epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations, reports relative risks (RRs) with appropriate statistical modeling, and appears to be published in English. While the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it explicitly includes respiratory admissions as an outcome of interest.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly mentioned as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is asthma-related ED visits which are respiratory ED visits, (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. Although the abstract primarily reports results for other pollutants (O3, CO, NO2), PM2.5 is clearly stated as one of the exposures examined in the study.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory disease hospitalizations. It uses a distributed lag nonlinear model (DLNM), which is appropriate for time-series analysis. The study reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5 and other pollutants. All inclusion criteria are met: original research, PM2.5 exposure included, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series design, quantitative effect estimates with CIs provided.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 source apportionment and health outcomes, (2) exposure is PM2.5 from various sources, (3) outcome is respiratory emergency department visits (asthma, pneumonia, acute URI), (4) uses a case-crossover study design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) is published in English. The focus on source apportionment does not disqualify it as PM2.5 is the primary exposure being analyzed.

This is an original ecological time-series study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations in children. It uses Poisson regression GAM with appropriate lag structure and reports quantitative effect estimates (89 additional hospitalizations per 5µg/m3 increment in PM2.5). While the abstract describes absolute increases rather than relative risks explicitly, time-series studies using Poisson regression typically report or can derive relative risk estimates. The study meets all key inclusion criteria: original epidemiological research, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series design, and quantitative effect estimates.

This is an original time-series epidemiological study that examines PM2.5 (among other exposures) and emergency hospital admissions for respiratory diseases. The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals. Although the primary focus is on coarse PM (PMc), the methods clearly state that PM2.5 was analyzed as part of the exposure assessment and controlled for in models, making PM2.5 one of multiple exposures analyzed. This meets inclusion criteria per the exception 'unless PM2.5 is one of multiple exposures analyzed.'

This is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design to examine the association between PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations. While the primary focus is on evaluating geo-imputation methodology, the study reports hazard ratios (HRs) for the PM2.5-respiratory hospitalization association. It meets all inclusion criteria: original research, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, case-crossover design, and reports effect estimates (HRs) with information about their precision.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using Poisson time-series regression, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes respiratory hospital admissions, (4) study design is time-series, (5) reports effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals for respiratory hospitalizations, and (6) published in English. While the study also examines mortality and cardiovascular outcomes, it explicitly analyzes hospital admissions due to respiratory causes including COPD and asthma, which are relevant to the review.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a time-stratified case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) respiratory ED visits (specifically asthma) are among the outcomes examined, (4) the study design is case-crossover, (5) quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals are reported (OR = 1.13, 95% CI: 1.03-1.23 for PM2.5 and asthma), and (6) the article appears to be published in English. While the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes and other pollutants, this does not disqualify it from inclusion as PM2.5 and respiratory ED visits are clearly analyzed.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) exposure is PM2.5 (wildfire-sourced), (3) outcome includes respiratory ED visits, (4) time-series design explicitly stated, (5) reports effect estimates with 95% CI (0.47% increase per 1 μg/m3 increment for respiratory diseases, 95% CI: 0.30%, 0.64%), and (6) published in English. Although the PM2.5 is specifically from wildfire sources, it is still PM2.5 exposure which meets the inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure, reports respiratory hospitalizations (asthma admissions) as the outcome, provides quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (12% and 3% elevation in admissions), and appears to be published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as an exposure, (3) respiratory hospitalizations are included as outcomes (lower respiratory tract infections and COPD), (4) case-crossover design is specified, (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals are reported (e.g., 2.8% increase for lower respiratory tract infections, 1.6% for COPD), and (6) published in English. Although the study also examines cardiac outcomes and other particle sizes, it clearly reports PM2.5 effects on respiratory hospitalizations with effect estimates.

This is an original time-series study examining the association between short-term PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations (as well as circulatory). The study reports quantitative effect estimates with credible intervals for both respiratory and circulatory outcomes. It meets all inclusion criteria: original epidemiological research, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory hospitalization outcome, time-series design, and reports effect estimates with confidence/credible intervals.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Original epidemiological study using two-stage time-series analysis, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as an exposure, (3) Hospital admissions for AECOPD (acute exacerbation of COPD) are respiratory hospitalizations, (4) Time-series study design is clearly stated, (5) Reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals (RR=1.093, 95% CI 1.06-1.13 for PM2.5), and (6) Published in English. Although the title mentions 'ecological study', the methods clearly describe a time-series analysis which is an accepted design for this review.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory hospitalizations (influenza hospital visits, ICD-10 J11). The study uses appropriate statistical methods (GLM with quasi-Poisson) and reports quantitative associations. While the abstract doesn't explicitly state effect estimates with confidence intervals, the methods and results sections indicate these were calculated. The focus on interactive effects with viral exposure is a specific research question but doesn't disqualify the study from examining the PM2.5-hospitalization association.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original ecological time series study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations, and reports relative risk estimates with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., 6% increase with 95%CI: 1.4-10.8 for children; 6.8% increase with 95%CI: 0.5-13.5 for elderly).

This study meets most inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure (among other pollutants), includes respiratory hospitalizations and ED visits as outcomes (COPD mentioned specifically), uses Poisson regression with rate ratios and confidence intervals, and appears to use a time-series design based on short-term impacts and temporal adjustments. While it examines multiple chronic diseases and multiple pollutants, it does analyze PM2.5 specifically and includes respiratory outcomes (COPD hospitalizations/ED visits). The study design appears to be time-series based on the methodology described.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of multiple exposures, (3) respiratory hospitalization is reported as an outcome, (4) case-crossover design is clearly stated, (5) quantitative effect estimates with ranges (confidence intervals) are provided for PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalization (0.19%-0.69% and 0.33%-1.1% increase in odds), and (6) the article appears to be in English. Although it is a multi-pollutant study, PM2.5 results are separately reported for respiratory hospitalization.

This is an original time-series study using Poisson regression with DLNM to examine the association between PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory hospitalizations (AECOPD). The study reports quantitative effect estimates including relative cumulative risks and percentage increases in hospitalizations per 10 μg/m3 increase in pollutants. COPD exacerbations are a respiratory hospitalization outcome. All inclusion criteria are met.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and includes respiratory outcomes (ARDS, pneumonia) among hospitalized patients with quantitative effect estimates, it fails to meet the study design criterion. This is a cohort study examining chronic air pollution exposure and COVID-19 morbidities among hospitalized patients, not a time-series or case-crossover design. The study follows hospitalized COVID-19 patients and examines outcomes conditional on already being hospitalized, rather than examining the association between short-term PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations in the general population.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) respiratory hospitalizations (ICD-10: J00-J99) are included as an outcome, (4) time-series design is clearly stated, (5) the abstract indicates Poisson regression models were fitted which would provide effect estimates, though specific RR/OR values are not shown in the abstract. The study analyzes multiple pollutants including PM2.5, which is acceptable per inclusion criteria that allow PM2.5 as one of multiple exposures.

This study meets most inclusion criteria: it is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 exposure and pneumonia hospitalizations (a respiratory outcome). However, the abstract does not explicitly report quantitative effect estimates (RR, OR, or equivalent with confidence intervals), only stating that associations were statistically significant (P<0.05) and describing relative rankings of pollutant effects. Without confirmation that specific effect estimates with CIs are reported in the full text, the study cannot be definitively included based on criterion 5.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Original epidemiological study using generalized additive models; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly listed as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) Outcome is COPD hospital admissions, which is a respiratory hospitalization; (4) Study design is time-series based on the methodology described (GAM with lag effects, controlling for temporal trends); (5) Reports percentage change in hospital admissions per 10 µg/m³ increase, which is a quantitative effect estimate; (6) Published in English. COPD hospitalizations are a specific type of respiratory hospitalization that fits the outcome criteria.

While this is an original case-crossover study examining respiratory ED visits with quantitative effect estimates, the exposure is PM10 and PM2.5-10 (coarse particles between 2.5-10 µm), not PM2.5 (fine particles ≤2.5 µm). The study explicitly states it assessed PM10 and PM2.5-10 contained in Saharan dust, and does not report separate analyses for PM2.5 exposure, which is the required exposure for this systematic review.

While this is an original case-crossover study that includes PM2.5 exposure and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals, the outcome is clinically defined COPD exacerbations experienced in patients' homes, not respiratory hospitalizations or ED visits. The abstract explicitly states these exacerbations were detected early in a disease management program before they resulted in ED visits or hospital admissions.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is asthma hospital admissions (respiratory hospitalization), (4) time-series design explicitly stated, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs (3% increase per 1 μg/m3 PM2.5, 95% CI 1.006% to 1.052%), and (6) published in English. Although multiple pollutants are examined, PM2.5 is specifically analyzed and reported.

While this study meets most inclusion criteria (original epidemiological study, respiratory hospitalization outcome, appropriate study designs, effect estimates with CIs), the primary exposure of interest is coarse particulate matter (PM10-2.5), not PM2.5. The abstract explicitly states 'We did not find significant effects of fine particulate matter (PM2.5)' on asthma hospitalizations. Although PM2.5 was analyzed, it was not the main exposure and showed null findings, making this study inappropriate for a systematic review specifically focused on PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Original epidemiological study using generalized additive models; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly studied as an exposure; (3) Emergency department visits for COPD exacerbations (respiratory outcome); (4) Time-series design with lag analysis; (5) Reports quantitative effect estimates (5.8% increase per 10 µg/m³ PM2.5 with attributable fraction); (6) Published in English. The study design is described as 'ecological' but the methodology (GAM with lag structure, adjustment for weather, time-series of ED visits) is consistent with a time-series analysis.

While this study examines PM2.5 among other pollutants and reports respiratory hospitalizations as an outcome with relative risk estimates, it is described as a 'spatio-temporal ecological study' rather than a time-series or case-crossover design. The study design does not meet the inclusion criteria requiring specifically time-series or case-crossover methodology. Additionally, the abstract emphasizes NO2 results rather than PM2.5 findings.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) exposure is wildfire-specific PM2.5, (3) outcomes include both respiratory hospitalizations and ED visits, (4) case-crossover study design, (5) reports OR with 95% CI (OR=1.014, 95% CI=1.012-1.016) for respiratory diseases, and (6) published in English. While the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it separately reports results for respiratory diseases which are relevant to the review.

The study meets most inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using time-series analysis, examines PM2.5 exposure, and reports respiratory hospitalizations and ER visits as outcomes. However, the abstract does not explicitly state whether a quantitative effect estimate (RR, OR, or equivalent) with confidence intervals was reported - it only mentions 'statistically significant association (p < 0.05)'. Without confirmation that specific effect estimates with CIs are provided in the full text, the study cannot be definitively included per criterion 5.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory ED visits. It reports quantitative effect estimates (IRR). Although the outcome is upper respiratory tract infections specifically (rather than all respiratory conditions), URTI is a respiratory condition leading to ED visits, which meets the outcome criteria. PM2.5 was analyzed as one of multiple exposures with effect estimates reported.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory emergency department visits in Atlanta from 1993-2004. The study uses Poisson generalized linear models and reports associations (effect estimates) between pollutants and respiratory ED visits. It meets all inclusion criteria: original epidemiological study, includes PM2.5 exposure, respiratory ED visits as outcome, time-series design, and reports quantitative effect estimates with positive associations mentioned for multiple pollutants.

This is an original time-series study that includes PM2.5 as an exposure variable and respiratory hospitalizations as an outcome. The study reports relative and attributable risks calculated using generalized linear models. While the study examines multiple pollutants and outcomes, it specifically mentions NO2 associations with respiratory disease admissions and asthma-related admissions, and PM2.5 is listed as one of the exposures analyzed. The study meets all inclusion criteria despite being a multi-exposure, multi-outcome study.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and asthma hospitalizations using time-series analysis with Poisson regression, the results explicitly state that 'no significant associations were found for PM2.5...with asthma-related...hospitalizations.' This suggests no quantitative effect estimate (RR, OR, or equivalent with confidence interval) for the PM2.5-asthma hospitalization association was reported. The study appears to be primarily focused on surveillance capacity building and describing disparities rather than reporting specific effect estimates for PM2.5 and respiratory outcomes.

While this is an original time-series study examining respiratory hospitalizations and ED visits with quantitative effect estimates, the primary exposure is PM10, not PM2.5. Although the abstract mentions PM10 is 'mostly PM2.5', the actual exposure measured and analyzed is PM10, and the effect estimates reported are for PM10 (per 100 µg/m3 increase in PM10). The study does not report separate PM2.5 measurements or PM2.5-specific effect estimates, which is required for inclusion.

While this study meets several inclusion criteria (original epidemiological study, PM2.5 exposure, time-series design, quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals), the outcome is doctors' house calls for respiratory diseases rather than respiratory hospitalizations or emergency department visits. The study explicitly distinguishes house calls from hospital admissions, making it incompatible with the specified outcome criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using a generalized additive model on daily hospital admissions data; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) the outcome is respiratory hospital admissions; (4) the study design is time-series (daily hospital admissions analyzed over 4 years with lag structures); (5) quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals are reported (0.885% increase per 10μg/m3 PM2.5, 95%CI: 0.414%~1.358%); and (6) the abstract is in English. While multiple pollutants are examined, PM2.5 is specifically analyzed and reported.

Although this is an original case-crossover study examining PM2.5 exposure with quantitative effect estimates, the outcome is respiratory mortality, not respiratory hospitalization or emergency department visits as required by the inclusion criteria. The study specifically focuses on deaths from respiratory diseases rather than hospital admissions.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) the outcome is respiratory hospitalization (asthma hospital admissions), (4) it uses a time-series study design with DLNM, (5) it reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals for multiple pollutants including PM2.5, and (6) the article is published in English. Although the abstract primarily highlights NO2 results, it clearly states that PM2.5 was analyzed and found to have effects on childhood asthma admissions.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) Original epidemiological study using GAM time-series analysis; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) AECOPD hospitalization is a respiratory outcome; (4) GAM indicates time-series design; (5) Reports relative risk (RR) with analysis of hospitalization risk; (6) Published in English. While the study examines multiple pollutants and multiple health outcomes (including non-respiratory), it includes PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalization (AECOPD) with quantitative effect estimates.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological time-series study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory (asthma) hospital admissions, reports relative rates with 95% confidence intervals (RR=1.04, 95% CI=1.02-1.07 for PM2.5), and uses Poisson regression with appropriate controls for temporal trends and confounders.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations (AECOPD admissions). It uses a time-series design (Poisson generalized additive model with temporal adjustments), reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs for PM2.5, and the outcome is respiratory hospitalization. The only minor concern is that the title is in Chinese brackets suggesting possible translation, but the abstract is in English and meets all inclusion criteria.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations using a generalized additive model (consistent with time-series design). The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs (e.g., 0.2% increase per 10 µg/m3 PM2.5 with 95% CI: 0.1-0.7%, and RR values). The outcome is respiratory hospital admissions, exposure includes PM2.5, and the study appears to be published in English. All inclusion criteria are met.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure includes PM2.5 (along with PM10), (3) outcome includes respiratory ED visits (asthma, COPD, respiratory conditions), (4) case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. Although the exposure is defined as smoke events based on both PM10 and PM2.5, PM2.5 is explicitly mentioned as one of the exposure metrics used.

This is a longitudinal birth cohort study, not a time-series or case-crossover design. The exposure (PM2.5 components) was assigned based on postal codes at birth and children were followed for 13 years, which is characteristic of a cohort study examining long-term exposure effects rather than short-term temporal associations. The inclusion criteria specifically require time-series or case-crossover designs.

While this is an original case-crossover study examining respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits with quantitative effect estimates, the primary exposure is ozone, not PM2.5. Although PM2.5 (fine particulate matter) is mentioned as a co-pollutant that was adjusted for, the study's focus and reported results are for ozone exposure. The inclusion criteria require PM2.5 as the primary exposure of interest.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) includes PM2.5 as one of the exposures analyzed with specific effect estimates reported, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization (asthma and bronchiolitis), (4) case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (OR: 1.22, 95% CI=1.03-1.44 for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Although the study also examines other exposures (SO2 and wind direction), PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed with quantitative effect estimates.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and includes respiratory hospitalizations as an outcome using Poisson regression (time-series design), it appears to be a health impact assessment that estimates attributable cases rather than reporting relative risks or odds ratios with confidence intervals. The 95% CI reported (204-749 million RMB) refers to economic losses, not epidemiological effect estimates. The study reports absolute numbers of cases attributed to pollution rather than quantitative effect measures (RR/OR) per unit increase in PM2.5.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using time-series analysis to examine the association between PM2.5 (among other particulate matter measures) and respiratory hospitalizations among elderly adults. The study reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals. Although the main finding indicates no significant association between PM2.5 and respiratory admissions, PM2.5 was explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures, making it relevant for the systematic review.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure (from wildfire smoke) and emergency department visits for respiratory outcomes including asthma exacerbation and unspecified respiratory disorder. The study uses time-series methodology with distributed lag models, reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals, and meets all inclusion criteria. While it also examines cardiovascular outcomes, it includes respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits as primary outcomes of interest.

The study meets several inclusion criteria: it uses time-series analysis, examines PM2.5 exposure, and assesses respiratory hospitalizations. However, the abstract describes this as an intervention study evaluating the effect of a heating technology substitution program rather than a traditional epidemiological study examining the direct association between PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations. The abstract does not clearly indicate whether quantitative effect estimates (RR, OR, or equivalent with confidence intervals) linking PM2.5 levels to hospitalizations are reported, or whether it only describes changes in PM2.5 levels and hospitalization rates before/after the intervention. Full text review would be needed to determine if this reports the PM2.5-hospitalization association with appropriate effect measures.

While this is a time-series study that includes PM2.5 as an exposure and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals for respiratory hospital admissions, the primary exposure is the composite Air Quality Health Index (AQHI) rather than PM2.5 specifically. The study does not report individual PM2.5 effects on respiratory hospitalizations, which is the focus of the systematic review. The AQHI combines multiple pollutants (SO2, NO2, O3, PM2.5) into a single index, making it impossible to isolate the PM2.5-respiratory hospitalization association.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original case-crossover epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly measured as an exposure, (3) respiratory hospitalizations are examined as outcomes (including COPD, pneumonia, and asthma), (4) uses case-crossover design with conditional logistic regression, (5) reports associations/effect estimates for respiratory outcomes, and (6) published in English. While the abstract does not explicitly state confidence intervals, the use of conditional logistic regression in a case-crossover study and mention of 'significant associations' strongly suggests quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals were calculated.
The outcome is atrial fibrillation (AF) hospitalization, which is a cardiovascular condition, not respiratory hospitalization or ED visit. This does not meet inclusion criterion #3.

The study examines myocardial infarction (MI) hospitalizations as the outcome, not respiratory hospitalizations. Additionally, the exposure is PM10 (particulate matter <10 µm), not PM2.5 (particulate matter ≤2.5 µm). Both the exposure and outcome do not meet the inclusion criteria.

While this is an original time-series study that includes PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations as outcomes, the primary focus is on temperature-hospitalization associations and how air pollutants modify these temperature effects. The study does not report direct effect estimates (RR/OR) for the association between PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations. Instead, it examines interaction/modification effects between temperature and pollutants. The effect estimates provided are for temperature effects stratified by pollution levels, not for PM2.5-respiratory hospitalization associations.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and emergency department visits for pediatric asthma exacerbations. Rate ratios were estimated from time-series models. While the primary focus is on comparing different exposure characterization methods, it meets all inclusion criteria: original epidemiological study, includes PM2.5 exposure, respiratory ED visits as outcome, time-series design, and reports rate ratios with statistical measures.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure includes fine particulate matter (PM2.5), (3) outcome includes respiratory hospitalizations (asthma, COPD), (4) time-series design explicitly stated, (5) quantitative effect estimates reported (4.6% increase for asthma, 4.3% for COPD per 10 µg/m3 PM2.5), and (6) published in English. While the study also examines cardiovascular outcomes and other pollutants, it specifically reports PM2.5-respiratory hospitalization associations which are directly relevant to the review.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and mentions respiratory outcomes (asthma, chronic bronchitis) and hospitalization, it appears to be primarily a health economic evaluation study focused on calculating economic losses rather than reporting epidemiological effect estimates (RR, OR) for the association between PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations. The abstract reports economic losses in yuan and number of cases, but does not provide relative risk or odds ratios with confidence intervals for the PM2.5-hospitalization association, which is required for inclusion.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome includes hospitalizations and ED visits for asthma/wheeze (respiratory conditions), (4) case-crossover study design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (e.g., OR: 1.08, 95% CI: 1.01, 1.15), and (6) published in English. Asthma and wheeze are respiratory conditions and the outcomes explicitly include hospitalizations and ED visits.

The study meets most inclusion criteria: it is a time-series analysis examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory hospital admissions. However, the abstract does not explicitly state whether quantitative effect estimates (RR, OR, or equivalent with confidence intervals) are reported. The abstract mentions 'significant association' but does not provide the actual effect measures, which is a key inclusion criterion. Full text review would be needed to confirm the presence of effect estimates.

This is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design to examine the association between PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and emergency department visits for pediatric asthma. The study reports quantitative effect estimates (RR: 1.10, 95% CI: 1.05, 1.16) for PM2.5 exposure. Although the primary focus is on demonstrating a methodological approach (regression trees) and examining multipollutant mixtures, it meets all inclusion criteria: original research, PM2.5 as one of the exposures, respiratory ED visits as outcome, case-crossover design, and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is asthma emergency department visits (respiratory ED visits), (4) time-series design explicitly stated, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates (4% increase in asthma ED visits associated with PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Although the abstract does not explicitly mention confidence intervals, it reports percentage increases which are quantitative effect estimates typical of time-series analyses.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations (influenza and pneumonia) using a time-series design (GAM/DLNM) and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals, the outcome measure is hospitalization COSTS rather than hospitalization incidence or counts. The study reports percentage increases in costs (0.89% cost increase per 10 µg/m³ PM2.5), not relative risk or odds ratios for hospitalization events. This does not meet the inclusion criteria which specifically requires respiratory hospitalization or ED visits as the outcome, not economic burden.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as an exposure, (3) outcome is ED visits for pneumonia which is a respiratory condition, (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals (14.0% increase, 95% CI 5.1-23.8% for PM2.5), and (6) published in English. Pneumonia is a respiratory condition requiring emergency care, which qualifies as respiratory ED visit.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly examined as an exposure, (3) outcome is bronchiolitis hospitalization (a respiratory hospitalization), (4) uses time-stratified case-crossover method, and (5) reports quantitative effect estimates (26-41% increased risk for premature infants). The study examines bronchiolitis, which is a respiratory condition requiring hospitalization, making it appropriate for a review on respiratory hospitalizations.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations. The study uses daily ZIP code counts with Poisson regression (time-series design), reports quantitative effect estimates (percent increases with IQR), includes respiratory admissions as an outcome, and appears to be published in English. While it also examines cardiac and stroke admissions, respiratory hospitalizations are explicitly included and analyzed.

This is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure (along with O3) and respiratory hospitalizations in Beijing using conditional Poisson regression (appropriate for time-series analysis). The study reports quantitative effect estimates including relative excess risk due to interaction with 95% CI (1.65%, 95%CI: 0.46%-2.84%). Although the study focuses on the interaction between PM2.5 and O3, PM2.5 is clearly one of the primary exposures analyzed, meeting inclusion criteria. The outcome is respiratory hospital admissions, the design is time-series based on the conditional Poisson regression approach, and effect estimates with confidence intervals are provided.

This is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 exposure (in Los Angeles County) and respiratory hospitalizations for COPD. The study uses generalized additive models to analyze daily hospital admissions, which is appropriate for time-series analysis. Although PM2.5 was only measured in one of three counties, the abstract indicates effect estimates were calculated (coefficients mentioned). COPD admissions qualify as respiratory hospitalizations. The study appears to report quantitative effect estimates even though specific RR/OR values are not provided in the abstract.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) exposure is PM2.5, (3) outcome is respiratory emergency department visits, (4) time-series study design, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (0.84%; 95% CI, 0.33-1.35% per 10-μg/m3 increase), and (6) published in English. No exclusion criteria apply.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization, (4) case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5 and other pollutants, (6) published in English. Although PM2.5 showed no significant effects in the multi-pollutant model, the study still examined PM2.5 exposure and reported quantitative effect estimates, making it eligible for inclusion.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study using time-series analysis, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) the outcome includes respiratory emergency department visits, (4) the study design is time-series, (5) the abstract indicates statistically significant percentage increases were reported (quantitative effect estimates), and (6) the publication is in English. While the study also examines other pollutants and circulatory outcomes, PM2.5 and respiratory ED visits are specifically analyzed and reported.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) exposure includes PM2.5 (along with PM2.5-bound metallic elements), (3) outcome is asthma emergency department visits (respiratory ED visits), (4) case-crossover study design, (5) reports statistically significant risk estimates with conditional logistic regression models, and (6) published in English. Although the study focuses on PM2.5-bound metallic elements, PM2.5 itself is analyzed and reported as an exposure with effect estimates.

This study meets the key inclusion criteria: (1) it is an original epidemiological study examining PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospital visits; (2) uses a time-series design with Poisson regression; (3) examines respiratory outcomes (ARI and pneumonia hospital visits); (4) analyzes PM2.5 concentration alongside oxidative potential metrics. While the abstract does not explicitly state effect estimates with confidence intervals, the use of Poisson regression models and description of 'significant correlations' and 'notable associations' strongly suggests quantitative effect estimates are reported in the full text. The study appears to be published in English and meets all other inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure (among other pollutants), reports respiratory hospitalizations as the outcome, and provides quantitative effect estimates (ORs with 95% CIs). The study explicitly reports OR=1.0179 (95% CI 1.0097-1.0260) for PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using time-series design, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of the exposures, (3) outcome is asthma-related emergency hospital admissions which is a respiratory hospitalization, (4) time-series approach is clearly stated, (5) reports relative risks with 95% confidence intervals for PM2.5 (RR 1.01, 95% CI 1.0003-1.03 for 5 µg/m3 increase), and (6) published in English. Although the outcome is specific to asthma rather than all respiratory conditions, asthma hospitalizations are a subset of respiratory hospitalizations and are commonly included in such reviews.

This is a simulation study, not an original epidemiological study with real health outcome data. The respiratory ED visits were simulated using Monte Carlo methods rather than observed from actual patient data. While it uses time-series methodology and includes PM2.5 as one of the exposures, it does not meet the inclusion criterion of being an original epidemiological study that reports actual associations between PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations.

While this is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 exposure, the outcome is medication purchase/sales rather than respiratory hospitalization or emergency department visits. The study does not meet inclusion criterion 3, which specifically requires respiratory hospitalization or ED visit as the outcome.

While this is an original time-series study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory hospitalizations for asthma, the abstract explicitly states that 'calculating relative risk inappropriate' and the results section only reports significant associations for NO2, not PM2.5. No quantitative effect estimate (RR, OR, or CI) for PM2.5 is reported in the abstract, which is a critical inclusion requirement.

The study examines cardiovascular hospitalizations, not respiratory hospitalizations. Although PM2.5 exposure is assessed and the study uses a case-crossover design with effect estimates, the outcome does not meet the inclusion criteria which specifically requires respiratory hospitalization or ED visits.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using DLNM; (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed; (3) outcome is respiratory hospitalization; (4) time-series design with daily data and lag analysis; (5) reports relative risk (RR) estimates with specific quantitative values for PM2.5 (0.23% increase in hospitalization risk per 10% increase in PM2.5 at 5-day lag); (6) published in English. Although multiple pollutants are examined, PM2.5 is specifically analyzed and reported.

This is an original time-series epidemiological study examining the association between PM2.5 (among other pollutants) and respiratory ED visits. The study reports associations between respiratory ED visits and ozone, and mentions fine particulate matter as one of the exposures analyzed. The study uses Poisson models to estimate health associations, which would provide effect estimates with confidence intervals. It meets all inclusion criteria: original research, includes PM2.5 exposure, includes respiratory ED visits as outcome, uses time-series design, and appears to report quantitative effect estimates.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and respiratory hospitalizations (COVID-19), the study design is a retrospective cohort study using patient-level data from hospital records, not a time-series or case-crossover design as required by the inclusion criteria. The study analyzes 208,744 individual patients admitted to hospitals, which is characteristic of a cohort design rather than analyzing aggregated time-series data or using case-crossover methodology.

Although this is an original case-crossover study examining PM2.5 exposure with quantitative effect estimates, the outcome is acute kidney injury (AKI) emergency department visits, not respiratory hospitalization or ED visits. The study does not meet the outcome inclusion criteria.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using quasi-Poisson regression with DLNM, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed as one of multiple exposures, (3) respiratory-related emergency hospital admissions are reported as an outcome, (4) time-series study design, (5) reports risk associations with quantitative effect estimates (positive associations with increased risk mentioned), and (6) published in English. While the study examines multiple pollutants and outcomes, it specifically reports on PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using GAM with Poisson regression, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly studied as one of the exposures, (3) outcome is emergency room visits for respiratory diseases, (4) time-series design indicated by GAM controlling for temporal trends and day-of-week effects, (5) reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% CIs for PM2.5 (1.4% increase per 10 μg/m³ in urban, 1.5% in suburban areas), and (6) published in English.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly included as one of the exposures analyzed, (3) outcome is emergency department visits for asthma (a respiratory condition), (4) uses case-crossover design, (5) reports odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. Although the abstract primarily reports results for O3, NO2, and PM10, PM2.5 is clearly stated as one of the pollutants examined.

Although this study meets criteria for exposure (PM2.5), study design (case-crossover), and has effect estimates with confidence intervals, the outcome is ED visits for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), which is a neurodegenerative disease, not a respiratory hospitalization or ED visit. The inclusion criteria specifically require respiratory hospitalization/ED visits as the outcome.

This is an original epidemiological study using an interrupted time-series design to examine the association between PM2.5 exposure (from wildfire smoke) and pediatric respiratory emergency department and urgent care visits. The study reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (excess respiratory visits per day). It meets all inclusion criteria: original research, PM2.5 exposure, respiratory ED/urgent care visits as outcome, time-series design, and reports effect estimates with CIs.

This is a long-term cohort/ecological study examining 12-year follow-up effects, not a time-series or case-crossover design. The study design involves exposure data from 1999-2000 and outcome data from 2012, which is characteristic of a cohort study examining long-term effects rather than short-term associations. The inclusion criteria specifically require time-series or case-crossover designs.

While this is an original time-series study examining respiratory hospitalizations with effect estimates, the primary exposure of interest is aeroallergens (tree pollen, fungi, weeds), not PM2.5. PM2.5 is used as a stratifying variable to examine effect modification rather than as the main exposure. The study does not report the direct association between PM2.5 and respiratory hospitalizations, which is the focus of the systematic review.

While this is a case-crossover study examining PM2.5 exposure with effect estimates reported, the primary outcome is mental health emergency department visits, not respiratory hospitalizations or ED visits. Although respiratory mortality is mentioned in the results, it is not the focus of the study and no specific effect estimate for respiratory outcomes is provided.

While this study examines PM2.5 as one of multiple exposures and reports respiratory ED visits as an outcome, the primary exposure of interest is influenza, not PM2.5. The study uses time-series models to estimate influenza-attributable respiratory ED visits, then uses spatial models to examine correlates (including PM2.5) of this influenza burden. PM2.5 is treated as a covariate/correlate rather than the primary exposure. The study design does not directly assess the association between PM2.5 and respiratory ED visits in the manner required for inclusion.

This is an original epidemiological study using time-series design (Poisson regression models with daily counts) that examines PM2.5 as one of multiple exposures. The study reports respiratory hospitalizations as an outcome with quantitative effect estimates and 95% confidence intervals. Although the primary focus is on ultrafine particles, PM2.5 is explicitly analyzed and reported with effect estimates for respiratory hospital admissions. The study meets all inclusion criteria.

This is an original time-series epidemiological study examining PM2.5 (among other pollutants) in relation to respiratory ED visits including asthma and COPD. The study reports statistically significant associations which implies effect estimates were calculated. Although the abstract does not explicitly state RR/OR with confidence intervals, it describes appropriate statistical modeling (GLM, GEE, GAM) and reports significant positive associations for respiratory outcomes. PM2.5 and its components were explicitly measured and analyzed during the superstation period.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure and pediatric asthma hospitalizations, it does not meet the inclusion criteria for study design (not time-series or case-crossover) and does not report the required effect measure. The study uses Poisson and linear regression to examine associations between monthly average pollutant concentrations and hospitalization costs/charges/length of stay, but does not report RR, OR, or equivalent measures for respiratory hospitalization risk. The outcome is primarily economic (costs and charges) rather than hospitalization incidence or counts.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study, (2) PM2.5 is explicitly measured as one of multiple air pollutants, (3) outcome is respiratory ED visits for asthma/wheeze, (4) uses Poisson time-series design, (5) reports rate ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and (6) published in English. Although the abstract primarily highlights ozone results, PM2.5 and its components are clearly analyzed as exposures.

This is an original time-series epidemiological study that examines PM2.5 (among other pollutants) as an exposure and respiratory ED visits as an outcome. The study uses generalized additive models on time-series data from 1992-1996. The abstract explicitly mentions PM2.5 in single-pollutant models showing positive effects on respiratory diagnosis groups, and reports quantitative effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals. Although the final multipollutant model emphasizes O3 and SO2, PM2.5 results are reported in single-pollutant models, meeting the inclusion criteria.

While this study examines PM2.5 exposure using a time-series design with effect estimates, the primary outcome is 'critical illness' admissions to ED (Emergency Severity Index levels 1 and 2), not specifically respiratory hospitalizations. Although respiratory diseases are mentioned as one subgroup analysis among cardiovascular and neurological disorders, the main outcome encompasses all critical illness admissions. The study does not report separate effect estimates specifically for respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits, which is required for inclusion.

This is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design to examine PM2.5 exposure and emergency department visits. While the study reports no significant association for overall respiratory outcomes, it does examine respiratory ED visits (upper respiratory infections) as one of multiple outcomes and provides relative risk estimates with confidence intervals. The study meets all inclusion criteria: original research, PM2.5 exposure, includes respiratory ED visits as an outcome, case-crossover design, and reports effect estimates with CIs.

This is an original epidemiological study examining the association between PM2.5 (fine particulate matter) exposure and asthma emergency department visits in children. The study uses a time-series design (Poisson regression with daily ED counts regressed against air pollution). It reports a quantitative effect estimate (relative rate of 1.15 with 95% CI 1.08-1.23 for an 11 µg/m3 change in fine PM). Asthma ED visits are a respiratory outcome. All inclusion criteria are met.

While this study includes PM2.5 as one exposure measure, uses a time-series design, and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals, the primary outcome analyzed is mortality rather than respiratory hospitalization/ED visits. Although the abstract mentions 'hospital admissions of elderly patients' for respiratory conditions (pneumonia, COPD) were analyzed for 1992-1994, no specific effect estimates for respiratory hospitalizations are reported in the abstract - only mortality estimates are provided. The study does not meet the outcome criterion requiring respiratory hospitalization as the primary outcome with reported effect estimates.

While this is an original case-crossover study examining PM2.5 exposure with effect estimates reported, the outcome is ambulance emergency calls (AECs) rather than respiratory hospitalizations or ED visits. The study mentions respiratory diseases-related AECs in the conclusion, but the primary outcome is ambulance calls, which precede and are distinct from actual hospitalizations or ED visits. The study does not specifically report effect estimates for respiratory hospitalizations or ED visits.

The study includes PM2.5 exposure, respiratory ED visits (asthma), and appears to use time-series methods. However, the primary focus is on characterizing pollutant interactions and multi-collinearity rather than reporting health effect estimates. The asthma ED visit analysis is described as 'an example' provided at the end. It's unclear whether quantitative effect estimates with confidence intervals are reported for PM2.5 and respiratory outcomes, or if this is primarily a methodological paper about pollutant correlations. The abstract suggests the health analysis may be secondary/illustrative rather than the main objective.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: (1) original epidemiological study using case-crossover design, (2) PM2.5 exposure clearly specified with thresholds, (3) respiratory ED visits as outcome, (4) case-crossover study design, (5) mentions odds ratios from conditional logistic regression, and (6) published in English. The abstract indicates quantitative effect estimates were calculated ('increased odds'), though specific values are not provided in the abstract.

While this is an original time-series study examining respiratory hospitalizations/ED visits with a quantitative effect estimate (RR=1.23, 95% CI 1.07-1.41), the primary exposure is PM2.5 zinc composition rather than PM2.5 mass concentration itself. The study specifically investigates the metal component (zinc) of PM2.5, not overall PM2.5 levels, which does not meet the exposure criteria for a systematic review focused on PM2.5 exposure.

This study meets all inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using a case-crossover design, examines PM2.5 exposure, reports respiratory hospitalizations as the outcome, and provides multiple odds ratios with confidence intervals (e.g., 1.87(1.17-2.97) for asthma, 2.18(1.20-3.97) for LRTI). The study is published in English and reports quantitative effect estimates.

This study meets several inclusion criteria: it is an original epidemiological study using time-series design (Poisson GAM), examines PM2.5 as one of multiple exposures, includes respiratory ED visits as one of the outcomes, and reports effect estimates with confidence intervals. However, the abstract only presents results for SO2 associations with neurologic and circulatory outcomes, not for PM2.5 or respiratory outcomes. The study likely contains PM2.5-respiratory ED visit associations in the full text since both were measured, but this cannot be confirmed from the abstract alone.
